To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) HPV testing is not appropriate for cervical cancer screening in women younger than 25 years, and that (2) HPV screening will not be sustainable in women older than 65 years due to low prevalence rates of HPV.

the cervical cancer screening and treatment strategies described by Denny and colleagues (1) will not be feasible in most settings and that the cervical cancer prevention strategies described by Derry and colleagues (2) will not be acceptable.
HPV screening is not appropriate for women younger than age 30 years and that HPV screening is likely to be inadequate in settings where HPV prevalence rates are higher than 25%.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the feasibility of cervical cancer prevention strategies that incorporate HPV testing and cytology and that would allow excision of all screen-and-treat positive lesions.

the development of a new generation of noncytology-based cervical cancer screening tests that will be able to be performed in the field, in real time, by minimally trained personnel, and that will provide immediate results that will allow immediate, definitive treatment.
the development of sustainable cervical cancer screening and treatment programs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cytological screen-and-treatment strategies, such as that described by Denny and colleagues (2), will not be feasible in the United States, but they will be feasible in many other settings.

cytology should be incorporated into screen-and-treat protocols for cervical cancer prevention, and HPV testing should be reserved for women older than 30 years and for women younger than that age who do not have an HPV test result that is satisfactory (5,6).

cytology-based screen-and-treat cervical cancer prevention strategies are feasible in any setting in which screen-and-treat that incorporates HPV testing has been demonstrated and that HPV testing is not appropriate for women younger than the age of 30 years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that it is possible to prevent cervical cancer in the developing world.
the use of HPV testing in the screening of women for cervical cancer is a cost-effective method of reducing cervical cancer incidence and mortality.
the cervical cancer is one of the major health problem in the developing country like India.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the current screening paradigm in the United States, which is based on the detection of precancerous lesions by Papanicolaousmearing, has been highly successful and has resulted in a dramatic reduction in the incidence and mortality from cervical cancer.
the use of a combination of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cytology can be used as a cervical screening strategy for women in developing countries.
there are many ways to prevent cervical cancer, and we need to be open to all of them.
